title: 3-Read Friday #73: Retrieval Practice, Smartphone Bans, and AI Art
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #73 is bookended by two technology-facing pieces, with a retrieval-practice thought experiment in between. Adam Robbins uses a thought experiment involving four students completing the same retrieval quiz in different ways to argue that the most defensible approach is one that maximises accountability and thinking, even though it produces less tidy written evidence in students' books. SouthGlosHead, an executive headteacher, gives a first-hand account of the year-long consultative process that led two of his primary schools to ban smartphones from the school gates, driven by police-led safeguarding workshops and a decisive parent survey. Claire Stoneman closes the issue with a polemical essay on AI-generated art, arguing that outsourcing creativity to generative AI risks hollowing out the very human effort and knowledge that make art and creativity possible in the first place. Barton's own framing - endorsing the smartphone ban piece as making the case 'better than I ever could' - signals where his own sympathies lie on the more contentious technology question.
points: Adam Robbins's thought experiment concludes that the student who writes brief, complete answers under time pressure (accountable but efficient) likely learns the most, while students who write elaborately-but-slowly, or who merely 'think' without writing, are harder to hold accountable for genuine retrieval.

SouthGlosHead's smartphone-ban case study: a parent survey at one school found 87% in favour of a ban (231 respondents, ~75% turnout), driven substantially by a police-led workshop on the safeguarding risks of unsupervised phone access.

SouthGlosHead's key policy compromise: banning phones from school (not banning ownership), allowing 'brick phones' for children who walk home alone, addressing both the safety and liberty objections raised by parents.

Claire Stoneman's central worry about generative AI and art: 'knowing empowers one to think, to question, to judge, to evaluate' - and AI-generated art short-circuits the hard-won knowledge that underlies genuine creativity and understanding.

A shared thread across the issue's technology pieces: both SouthGlosHead and Stoneman argue that unmediated, low-effort access to technology (phones, AI image generators) erodes something schools exist to protect - safety and attention in one case, knowledge and creative agency in the other.
quotes: Adam asks us to consider the output of four students during retrieval practice. Which one learns more? Which output do you encourage the most?
I am at the stage where I feel it is a no-brainer that all schools should ban smartphones. This post articulates the case better than I ever could.
In my recent AI chat, Neil Almond lamented whether today's children would appreciate paintings when they could generate something "better" at the click of a button. Claire develops this argument.
